yaml.title: Glossary and FAQ
yaml.subtitle: Key concepts on Theil indices and frequently asked questions

markdown.markdown:
Theil index $T_1$
: Generalised entropy index GE(1), proposed by Henri Theil (1967). It is more sensitive to differences at the **top** of the distribution. It is 0 under perfect equality and its maximum, $\ln n$, is reached when one person has all the income.

Theil index $T_0$ (mean log deviation, MLD)
: Generalised entropy index GE(0). It is the average of $\ln(\mu / y_i)$ and is more sensitive to differences at the **bottom** of the distribution. The World Bank publishes it for most countries.

Generalised entropy family GE($\alpha$)
: Family of inequality indices that includes $T_0$ ($\alpha = 0$) and $T_1$ ($\alpha = 1$). The parameter $\alpha$ sets the sensitivity to different parts of the distribution: the lower $\alpha$, the more weight on low incomes.

Additive decomposition
: Total inequality equals **between-group** inequality plus **within-group** inequality. Theil indices satisfy it exactly; the Gini index does not.

Between-group inequality
: Inequality that would remain if every person had the mean income of their group. It measures the gaps between groups (regions, sexes, sectors…).

Within-group inequality
: Weighted sum of the inequality inside each group: by population shares in $T_0$ and by income shares in $T_1$.

Bias of an estimator
: Difference between the average value of an estimator over all possible samples and the true value. Theil estimators are usually biased **downwards**.

Relative bias
: Bias divided by the true value, in percent. In THEILUMINA: negligible if below 2%, mild between 2% and 5%, moderate between 5% and 10%, and severe above 10%.

Skewness and heavy tails
: Income and wealth distributions have a long right tail: few people with very high values. The heavier the tail, the larger the bias and the harder the inference for inequality indices.

Jackknife
: Resampling method that recomputes the estimator leaving out one observation at a time. It estimates the bias and the variance of the estimator. THEILUMINA obtains closed-form expressions that compute it in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ operations.

Bootstrap
: Resampling method that draws many samples with replacement from the data to approximate the distribution of an estimator and build confidence intervals.

Delta method
: Approximation of the variance of an estimator based on a first-order Taylor expansion. It is fast, but can be unreliable with heavy-tailed distributions.

Confidence interval and coverage
: Range of values that contains the true value with a given probability (e.g. 95%). An interval has good **coverage** when that probability is achieved in practice.

Superpopulation
: Framework in which the observed data (even a census, such as all the countries in the world) are treated as a realisation of an underlying random process, which justifies statistical inference on them.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why use Theil indices instead of the Gini index?**
Because they can be decomposed exactly into between- and within-group inequality, and because the family offers indices with different sensitivity to the bottom ($T_0$) and the top ($T_1$) of the distribution. The Gini index remains useful and is often reported together with them.

**Should I use $T_0$ or $T_1$?**
It depends on the question. $T_0$ weights every person equally in the decomposition and is more sensitive to low incomes; $T_1$ weights by income shares and is more sensitive to high incomes. Reporting both is good practice.

**Can I compute Theil indices with zero or negative incomes?**
No: they use logarithms of income. Zero and negative values must be handled explicitly (excluded, bottom-coded or analysed with another index) and the number of affected observations should be reported.

**Is the bias important in practice?**
It can be. With small samples, small groups in a decomposition or very skewed distributions, the relative bias of the usual estimators can exceed 10%. Try the [bias explorer](simulation.qmd) or the [calculator](calculator.qmd) to see it.

**How can I obtain a margin of error for my index?**
With the jackknife or the bootstrap, or with linearisation if your data come from a survey with a complex design (e.g. the R package `convey`). The [calculator](calculator.qmd) and the [practical guide](guides/theil-indices-r.qmd) show how.

**Where can I find official data on inequality?**
In the [observatory](observatory.qmd) (Eurostat, World Bank and INE) and in the [links of interest](links.qmd).

**When will the theil R package be available?**
It is one of the main results of THEILUMINA (work package 4). Announcements will be published in the [blog](blog/index.qmd) and in the [news](news.qmd).

**Can I use the materials of this website in my classes?**
Yes, citing the source as indicated in [How to cite](cite.qmd).
